fields.expected: I found the posting through my own job search. I spend a lot of time reading listings closely because I built a Playwright-based application agent that pulls postings, checks eligibility, and queues them for me to review, so I end up reading more job descriptions than most people. Rilla stood out because the framing was specific: indexing the offline world, a product already in use at over 1000 organizations including The Home Depot and PulteGroup, and an engineering team expected to ship rather than sit adjacent to the product. Most postings I read describe a stack. This one described a problem, which is what made me stop and actually read it.

fields.expected: ClarityAtlas, the iOS product I co-founded Open Health Intelligence to build and serve as technical lead for. The hard technical piece was estimating sleep without a wearable. I built a passive sleep-estimation system from phone-interaction and motion signals, pulling HealthKit and Core Motion inputs like step count, gait speed, and movement patterns, and inferring sleep windows from them. I built the rest end to end in Swift and SwiftUI on Supabase, including a "Sleep Twins" backend that matched users on standardized behavioral features with a weighted distance function. We shipped it into a live pilot at Hopkins with 30+ users, got into the Pava Spark Accelerator and NSF I-Corps, and received a non-binding indication of roughly $75,000 for about 7 to 8 percent, which we chose not to pursue because we wanted the right long-term partners. The part I did not expect to matter as much as the code was everything around it: recruiting users, getting a meeting with President Daniels by knocking on the doors of Garland Hall until someone let us pitch, and explaining over and over why the thing should exist.

fields.expected: For the past year I have been obsessively reading about how scientific research gets funded and evaluated, which has nothing to do with writing code and has changed how I write it. I started from an observation at Hopkins: very capable people around me were funneling into consulting and banking without seeming especially interested in the work. I read through the history of research institutions, from patronage to the German research university to Bell Labs to the postwar NIH and NSF grant model to DARPA and Focused Research Organizations, and talked to researchers, administrators, and science-policy people. I went in believing grant-writing overhead was the main constraint. I now think the bigger effect is selection: researchers learn which ideas are legible enough to survive review and never attempt the ones that are hard to justify in advance. I also dropped an automated-reproducibility idea once I could not answer who would pay to surface problems in published work. Being forced to abandon two theses I liked made me much faster at killing my own technical assumptions when a user or a benchmark contradicts them.

fields.expected: It matches how I already work. Most of what I have built came out of long stretches in a room with people, not scheduled sprints. With ClarityAtlas, my cofounders and I were working on the product on the night of Lighting of the Quads, realized President Daniels was nearby, walked to Garland Hall, and knocked on locked doors until we got to pitch him. That only happens if you are physically around your team and treating the work as the default thing you are doing. I want to be somewhere that expects junior engineers to own real pieces of the system rather than close isolated tickets, and that expectation only works if I am in the room where decisions get made, hearing what customers said that morning and shipping against it that afternoon. Rilla has over 1000 customers already using the product, so the feedback loop is real rather than hypothetical. The trade I care about is ownership and speed against comfort, and I would rather be in an office in NYC six days a week on a problem that actually has users than optimize for anything else right now.
